lead: Amplifiers, filters, data converters and phase-locked loops have no truth table and no clean stuck-at model. Their outputs are continuous, so an analog block is judged by measuring its specifications and checking that each lies inside a tolerance window. Hard faults are opens and shorts; soft faults are drifts that pass a quick check but break a specification. Quick structural checks such as IDDQ, oscillation test and loopback sit beside converter measurements such as DNL, INL, SNR and ENOB. Every chip with an ADC, a DAC or a radio needs them.
prereq: You need: test cost from 6.1, the test levels from 6.8, and ADC and DAC basics from an analog electronics course.

sections.h3: Why digital test methods stop at the analog boundary

blocks.text: A digital line has two values and a stuck-at model, so ATPG can aim at one fault (6.3). An analog node can sit at any voltage, and its correct value is a range: gain 10 ± 0.2, offset below 5 mV, noise below 1 mV rms. Measurement noise and tester error use up part of that window. Few internal nodes can be brought out, because a probe adds capacitance and changes the circuit, and analog tester channels are expensive, so on a mixed-signal SoC the analog part can cost more test time than all the logic.

A hard (catastrophic) fault is an open, a short or a dead component. A soft (parametric) fault is a drift: a resistor 20 % off, a transistor with low gain, a leaky capacitor. The block may still work in a quick check but miss its specification, which is why analog test measures specifications, not only connections.

Quick structural checks find hard faults cheaply. IDDQ measures the quiescent supply current after the block settles; a short or bridge raises it. Oscillation test reconfigures a filter or amplifier into an oscillator; its frequency depends on the component values, so a shifted frequency points to a fault. Loopback sends a digital pattern through a DAC, the analog path and an ADC, and compares the returned codes with a tolerance.

sections.h3: Converter specifications and how they are measured

blocks.text: For an N-bit ADC with full-scale range FSR, 1 LSB = FSR ÷ 2N. Offset error is the shift of the whole transfer curve, in LSB; gain error is the error in its slope after offset is removed. Both are taken out before the linearity errors are found.
where DNLk is the differential nonlinearity of code k and Wk the measured width of that code in volts. DNLk = −1 LSB means Wk = 0: a missing code.
where INL<sub>k</sub> is the integral nonlinearity at the upper edge of code k, its distance from the ideal straight line in LSB; the INL quoted on a data sheet is the largest magnitude.

SNR is signal power over noise power, with the harmonics left out; SINAD is signal power over noise plus distortion. An ideal N-bit converter with a full-scale sine has SNR = 6.02N + 1.76 dB, and the effective number of bits is ENOB = (SINAD − 1.76) ÷ 6.02.

The servo method finds each code edge in turn with a feedback loop: accurate but slow. The histogram method applies a slow linear ramp (or a sine), counts how many samples land in each code, and turns counts into widths, so DNL and INL come out of simple counters. The FFT method applies a pure sine and transforms the output codes, giving SNR, THD, SINAD and ENOB. Histogram and FFT tests are the production standard.

sections.h3: Design for testability for analog blocks

blocks.text: Analog DFT adds access and control. Test points bring internal nodes out through unity-gain buffers so the probe does not load them. Bypass switches isolate a block, so the ADC can be tested without the filter in front of it. Loopback is the workhorse: digital pattern, on-chip DAC, analog path, on-chip ADC, digital compare. It catches opens, shorts, gross gain loss and filter shifts, but not every fault: a DAC gain 2 % high and an ADC gain 2 % low cancel in the returned code.

On-chip measurement puts a peak detector, an RMS detector or a small ADC beside the block, so the tester reads a number: this is analog BIST. IEEE 1149.4 extends boundary scan to analog pins: an analog boundary module switches each pin onto a two-wire internal analog test bus, and an external instrument connected to that bus forces a current or measures a voltage. It is mainly used for testing analog board wiring and discrete parts.

examples.question: An 8-bit ADC has a full-scale range of 2.56 V. A ramp histogram gives code widths W<sub>64</sub> = 14 mV and W<sub>65</sub> = 6 mV, and INL<sub>63</sub> = 0 LSB. (a) Find 1 LSB. (b) Find DNL at codes 64 and 65. (c) Find INL at codes 64 and 65. (d) A third code has a measured width of 0 mV; give its DNL and what it means.
steps: (c) INL<sub>64</sub> = INL<sub>63</sub> + DNL<sub>64</sub> = 0 + 0.4 = +0.4 LSB. INL<sub>65</sub> = 0.4 + (−0.4) = 0.0 LSB.
(d) DNL = 0 ÷ 10 − 1 = −1 LSB: the code never appears, a missing code. At that code INL drops by 1 LSB from the previous code's value; it looks near zero only if the previous INL was about +1 LSB.
Check: the two code widths add to 20 mV = 2 LSB, the same as two ideal codes, which is why INL returns to 0 after code 65.
examples.answer: 1 LSB = 10 mV; DNL<sub>64</sub> = +0.4 LSB and DNL<sub>65</sub> = −0.4 LSB; INL<sub>64</sub> = +0.4 LSB and INL<sub>65</sub> = 0.0 LSB; a 0 mV code has DNL = −1 LSB and is missing.

traps: Treating DNL and INL as the same. DNL is the error of one code width; INL is the running sum of DNL, the distance from the ideal line.
Writing a missing code as INL = −1 LSB. A missing code has DNL = −1 LSB; INL at that code falls by 1 LSB from its previous value.
Finding INL before removing offset and gain error. A tilted transfer curve is gain error, not a large INL.
Dividing by 2<sup>N</sup> − 1 for 1 LSB when the question defines FSR over 2<sup>N</sup> codes. Use FSR ÷ 2<sup>N</sup> unless told otherwise.
Calling SINAD 'SNR'. SNR leaves the harmonics out; SINAD includes them, and ENOB is computed from SINAD.

quiz.q: Define DNL and INL for an ADC.
quiz.a: DNL of code k is W<sub>k</sub> ÷ (1 LSB) − 1, the error of that code's width. INL at code k is the sum of DNL up to k, the distance of that code edge from the ideal straight line.

quiz.q: Distinguish a hard fault from a soft fault in an analog block.
quiz.a: A hard fault is catastrophic: an open, a short or a dead part. A soft fault is a parameter drift that leaves the block working but outside its specification.

quiz.q: Why can a soft parametric fault pass a quick functional check?
quiz.a: The block still responds, only with a slightly wrong gain, offset or noise; the quick check sees an output, and only a measurement against the specification window shows the drift.

quiz.q: A 10-bit ADC has FSR = 4.096 V. A code has a measured width of 5 mV. Find 1 LSB and the DNL of that code.
A 12-bit ADC measures SINAD = 68.0 dB. Find its ENOB and compare it with the ideal SNR.
quiz.a: ENOB = (68.0 − 1.76) ÷ 6.02 = 11.0 bits. Ideal SNR = 6.02 × 12 + 1.76 = 74.0 dB, so noise and distortion cost about one bit.

quiz.q: What does IEEE 1149.4 add to boundary scan?
quiz.a: Analog boundary modules at the pins and a two-wire analog test bus, so an external instrument on that bus can force a current or measure a voltage at a pin. It helps test analog board wiring and discrete parts.

quiz.q: Why can a loopback test pass when both the DAC and the ADC are out of specification?
quiz.a: Loopback compares only the final code with the pattern sent. If the DAC gain is 2 % high and the ADC gain 2 % low, the errors cancel and the code is right, although each block fails its own gain limit.

quiz.q: A code has DNL = −1 LSB but INL = 0.0 LSB at that code. Explain how.
quiz.a: The code is missing. The previous code's INL was +1.0 LSB, and adding DNL = −1 LSB brings the running sum back to 0. INL alone hides the missing code, so DNL must be checked too.

beyond: Not for the exam. High-speed serial links are tested with on-chip loopback and eye-diagram monitors; RF blocks are tested with modulated signals and spectral masks. Research moves measurement into the chip with on-chip instruments and uses machine learning to predict specifications from cheap measurements. Search 'ADC histogram test', 'analog BIST' and 'alternate test'.
